title: The Effects of Ocean Heat Uptake on Transient Climate Sensitivity
problem: This paper addresses the challenge of explaining why transient climate sensitivity increases over time in climate models, linking this behavior to the evolving spatial patterns of ocean heat uptake and its high-efficacy influence on cloud feedbacks, which are often not treated as interdependent processes.
method: To explain increasing transient climate sensitivity, the paper proposes a linear systems perspective that treats ocean heat uptake as a slowly-varying forcing whose high, spatially-dependent efficacy causes sensitivity to increase as the rate of heat uptake decays over time.
task: The task is to review and explain the physical mechanisms, particularly the role of ocean heat uptake and cloud feedbacks, that cause transient climate sensitivity to increase over time in climate models.
innovation: This paper proposes a physical mechanism in which the high efficacy of subpolar ocean heat uptake increases lower-tropospheric stability, enhancing low cloud feedbacks and causing transient climate sensitivity to increase over time as the heat uptake pattern evolves and decays.

For the sake of a concrete but idealized illustration, we adopt the aquaplanet CAM4 results of Rose et al. [53, 55] which define three responses ∆TCO2, ∆Tr, and ∆TH associated respectively with CO2, qT, and qH.

A slab ocean (SOM) version of CCSM4 has previously been used to assess equilibrium sensitivity in that model [6]. We calculated the equilibrium ∆EIS/ATs as the difference between 2×CO2 and 1×CO2 simulations in the SOM (black curve in Fig. 4).

Linear regression is used to calculate "effective radiative forcing” ERF (the intercept at ∆Ts = 0), “effective climate sensitivity” ∆Teff (extrapolation to equilibrium at AR = 0), and the feedback parameter λ (the slope in W m−2 K−1). This was the basis of the equilibrium climate sensitivity values reported in the IPCC AR5 [21]. Similar plots for other CMIP5 models appear in [3]. Such figures are colloquially known as “Gregory plots" in honor of their progenitor [27]. Figure 2 illustrates several long-running themes in the literature. The two models, CCSM4 and GFDL-CM3, disagree quantitatively on forcing, feedback, and climate sensitivity; however, both exhibit increasing sensitivity with time.
